title: Gray v. Powell (1941)
summary: When Congress assigns an agency the task of applying a statutory term such as producer to particular facts, a court respects the agency's conclusion if the hearing was fair and the statute was applied in a reasoned way.
notes:
Key line: "Where, as here, a determination has been left to an administrative body, this delegation will be respected and the administrative conclusion left untouched." Justice Reed, for the Court.

Citation: 314 U.S. 402 (1941).

sections.Parties: Petitioners were H. A. Gray, Director of the Bituminous Coal Division of the Department of the Interior, and the Division itself, which had denied the exemption. Respondents were the receivers of the Seaboard Air Line Railway Company, a coal-burning railroad that consumed large quantities of bituminous coal and claimed to be both producer and consumer of coal mined under its arrangements. The Government sought to bring the coal within the Bituminous Coal Code's price regulation. Seaboard sought to keep its coal outside the Code as captive coal consumed by its producer.
sections.Material Facts: The Bituminous Coal Act of 1937 imposed minimum and maximum prices on coal sold by code members and levied a 19.5 percent tax on coal disposed of by producers who were not members. Section 4-II(l) exempted coal consumed by the producer or transported by the producer to himself, and section 17(c) defined producer to include those engaged in the business of mining coal. Beginning in 1934 Seaboard leased coal lands at three mines, including the William-Ann Mine, and arranged for the landowners to lease the mining equipment to a contractor selected by Seaboard. The contractor, Daniel H. Pritchard, mined the coal at a per-ton price and delivered the entire output to Seaboard, managing the operation in his own way and bearing the operating risks, while Seaboard paid royalties to the landowners. Seaboard filed for an exemption on August 4, 1937, and the Director denied it on June 14, 1940.
sections.Procedural History: Seaboard sought review under section 6(b) of the Act in the Fourth Circuit, which reversed the Director and held that Seaboard was a producer entitled to the exemption. The Supreme Court granted certiorari and initially affirmed by an equally divided Court. It then granted rehearing, heard argument on October 21 and 22, 1941, and on December 15, 1941 reversed the Fourth Circuit and upheld the Director's order.
sections.Issue: The Bituminous Coal Act of 1937 exempted coal consumed by the producer from its price controls and defined producer to include those engaged in the business of mining coal. Seaboard did not mine coal with its own employees but arranged leases and an operating contract under which an independent contractor mined coal for its exclusive use. The Director found that Seaboard was not a producer. Should a reviewing court set aside that determination, and how much independent judgment may a court exercise when Congress has entrusted the application of a statutory term to an administrative body?
sections.Holding: No. Congress entrusted the determination of who is a producer to the specialized personnel of the Bituminous Coal Division. Where the agency has given a fair hearing with notice and opportunity to present arguments and has applied the statute in a just and reasoned manner, the court's function is complete and the administrative conclusion stands. The Director's conclusion that Seaboard was a consumer rather than a producer was reasonable. The judgment was reversed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Reed treated the question whether Seaboard was a producer as one that mixed law and fact and that Congress had deliberately assigned to an administrative body familiar with the coal industry. Congress followed a familiar practice in committing execution of its policies to specialized personnel, and where a determination has been left to an administrative body, that delegation is respected and the conclusion left untouched so long as the process was fair and the reasoning sound. The Court found ample support for the Director's view. Seaboard did not mine the coal itself; the contractor was an independent operator who managed the mine, hired the miners and bore the risks, and Seaboard's control was limited to price and inspection. The exemption for captive coal was meant for producers who consume their own output, and reading it to cover any consumer who arranged a supply contract would let large consumers escape the price structure and undermine the Act's purpose of stabilizing the industry. The Court also rejected the argument that section 4-II applies only where there is a sale, holding that disposal by consumption was enough, and held that Congress had power under the Commerce Clause to define producers for this purpose.

topics.lrs-i-independent-judgment: The Loper Bright opinions disagree over Gray’s implications for the pre-APA baseline.

learning.separateOpinions: The judgment was 7 to 1. Justice Roberts dissented, arguing that the record contained no disputed facts, that the Director made no factual finding but simply construed the statute, and that the meaning of a statute is a judicial question subject to full review. He read the exemption to cover Seaboard because the coal was produced for it and consumed by it without ever reaching the market. Justice Jackson took no part.
